Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Keep the supplied language.", "input": "The Saturday shift at the Harbor Street charity kitchen began before sunrise, while rain tapped against the loading-bay door and the street outside was still quiet. Mara, the shift coordinator, unlocked the pantry at 5:45 and checked the whiteboard before anyone started cooking. The plan was to serve lunch to about 140 people, but the number was only an estimate because the nearby shelter had reported several new arrivals overnight. Mara said, “Let’s prepare enough for the estimate, and keep the extra rice dry until we know how many guests are coming.” That decision mattered later, when the shelter called with an updated count.

Six volunteers arrived between six and six-thirty. Two had worked the kitchen before; the others were first-time helpers from a local college. Mara paired each new volunteer with someone who knew the room, then showed everyone where the hand-washing sink, gloves, fire blanket, and first-aid kit were kept. The kitchen’s printed temperature chart was clipped beside the refrigerator, and Leon checked the cooler before moving in the donated vegetables. It read 38 degrees Fahrenheit, within the kitchen’s safe range. A box of tomatoes had split during delivery, so the volunteers set aside the damaged fruit for immediate use rather than placing it in storage. The remaining produce was counted and recorded on the donation sheet.

The menu included lentil stew, rice, roasted carrots, bread, and apples. A donor had brought carrots from a neighborhood garden, along with a note saying they had been harvested the previous afternoon. Priya rinsed and peeled them while Ben cut them into even pieces. Mara asked the team to keep the vegetable scraps in the marked compost bin, not the regular trash. The lentils had already been sorted the night before, but the cooking group still rinsed them in batches and checked for small stones. When the large stockpot reached a steady simmer, Leon lowered the heat so the bottom would not scorch. He tasted a spoonful and said, “It needs a little more salt, but let’s wait until the broth has reduced.” Nobody added seasoning until the next tasting.

1. At 7:10, Mara divided the remaining preparation work. The first table washed and portioned apples, the second arranged bread in paper bags, and the third prepared labels for meals that needed to be carried to the shelter. Each label listed the meal’s date and the main ingredients. The kitchen did not claim that any meal was free of every possible allergen, so Mara told the volunteers to answer questions by checking the ingredient sheet rather than guessing. She also asked them to keep the serving spoons separate: one for the stew, one for the rice, and one for the carrots. A volunteer noticed that the handle on the rice spoon had a crack. Mara replaced it from the clean utensil drawer before service began.

The updated message from the shelter arrived at 8:20. It said that 18 additional people would need lunch, including several children, and asked whether the kitchen could send the meals by 11:30. Because the extra rice was still dry and the kitchen had enough lentils and broth, Mara approved cooking another pot. If the shelter had asked for more meals than the pantry could support, the team would have called the community center before changing the menu; in this case, there were enough ingredients, and the community center was not contacted. Two volunteers started the extra rice while Priya increased the stew batch. Mara wrote the new total on the whiteboard and told the packing team not to seal the shelter containers until the food had been counted.

At 9:15, a delivery driver arrived with bread that had been ordered for the following week. The invoice showed the later date, so Mara thanked him but did not accept the delivery into the day’s inventory. She called the bakery, and the manager confirmed that the order had been brought a week early by mistake. The driver took the crates back, leaving the kitchen with its original bread supply. That meant the team did not need to change the meal plan or borrow bread from another organization. Ben checked the remaining bags and found two with torn seams; those were kept for the volunteers’ staff meal, while intact bags were set aside for guests.

Service started at 11:45, fifteen minutes later than the shelter’s requested arrival time. The shelter driver had called to say that traffic was moving slowly near the bridge, so the packed containers stayed in the warming cabinet until the van arrived. The volunteers served guests at the kitchen’s front tables while Mara and Leon counted portions for the delivery. They packed 158 complete lunches, then counted the labels again before loading the van. “We have the right number, and the ingredient sheets are on top,” Leon said. Mara checked that the containers were closed and that the hot-food thermometer still showed a safe temperature. The driver signed the handoff sheet at 12:05 and carried the food to the shelter.

After the lunch rush, the team washed cookware, sanitized the counters, and recorded the remaining food. The lentil stew had run out, while some rice and roasted carrots remained. Mara cooled the leftovers according to the kitchen’s storage procedure, labeled the containers with the date and time, and placed them in the refrigerator. The cracked spoon was marked for disposal, and the delivery discrepancy was noted on the inventory form so the next shift would know why the bread count differed from the invoice. Before leaving, the volunteers checked the floor, emptied the compost bin, and returned the clean serving utensils to their drawer. Mara thanked each person by name and left the whiteboard updated for Sunday’s team: 158 lunches served, one early bread delivery returned, and the remaining rice and carrots stored for later use.", "output": "The Saturday shift at the Harbor Street charity kitchen began before sunrise, while rain tapped against the loading-bay door and the street outside was still quiet.
